title: Hubble 1929: The Linear Distance–Velocity Relation as a First Approximation
concept_summary: Hubble's 1929 paper reports a linear correlation between distances and radial velocities of extra-galactic nebulae. After solar-motion terms are removed, the simplified relation is v_corrected = K·d, where d is distance in Mpc and K is a historical slope in km/s/Mpc. The paper's fitted coefficients were 465 and 513, and it used a rounded intermediate value K = 500. This lesson lets you vary K and d to see that predicted corrected velocity is proportional to distance at fixed K, and that raising K steepens the line. The displayed line is a simplified mean relation, not a fit to or reproduction of observed nebular velocities.
why_it_matters: The distance–velocity relation is a foundational observational result in extragalactic astronomy. Understanding it as a linear first approximation over a restricted distance range — with scatter from peculiar motions and solar-motion corrections — is essential before encountering modern cosmological interpretations. The historical K = 500 is a rounded teaching value from 1929, not a present-day measurement of the Hubble constant.

explanation_steps.heading: A linear correlation in the data
explanation_steps.body: Hubble's paper states that the data indicate a linear correlation between distances and velocities. The relation is expressed through an equation of condition that includes solar-motion terms; once those angular terms are removed, the remaining distance term is v_corrected = r·K. In this lesson we rename r to d and treat K as an editable historical slope.

explanation_steps.heading: The historical slope values
explanation_steps.body: The paper reports two fitted historical coefficients, 465 and 513 km/s per million parsecs, and then adopts the rounded intermediate value K = 500. These are 1929 numbers, not current estimates. In the demo, K is a slider from 50 to 600 km/s/Mpc with default 500, so you can see how the predicted line changes with the slope.

explanation_steps.heading: A first approximation over a restricted range
explanation_steps.body: The final paragraph calls the linear relation a first approximation over a restricted distance range. The plotted corrected velocities still include residuals, and individual nebulae can deviate from the line because of peculiar motions. The exact line shown here is a simplified mean relation after solar-motion correction, not a fit to or reproduction of observed nebular velocities.

terms.meaning: Distance to a nebula in megaparsecs (Mpc); the source uses r in units of 10^6 parsecs.
Historical slope in km/s per Mpc; the paper's fitted values were 465 and 513, and it used the rounded value 500.
Radial velocity after removing solar-motion terms, in km/s; the simplified distance term is v_corrected = K·d.
The Sun's motion through space, described in the equation of condition by angular terms involving alpha and delta.
A galaxy's own motion relative to the mean expansion, which contributes scatter around the mean line.

equations.explanation: Simplified distance term after solar-motion correction: corrected radial velocity equals slope times distance. This is the teaching form of the paper's distance term.
Equation of condition from the paper, including solar-motion terms. The angular terms describe solar motion; after removing them, the simplified distance term is v_corrected = r*K.

controls.label: Historical slope K (km/s/Mpc)
controls.meaning: Editable historical slope. Default 500 is the paper's rounded intermediate value; 465 and 513 are the fitted coefficients.

controls.label: Distance d (Mpc)
controls.meaning: Distance to the nebula in megaparsecs. The line view sweeps this control from 0 to 10 Mpc.

computations.label: Predicted velocity at double the distance
Ratio of doubled-distance velocity to current velocity

visualizations.title: Predicted corrected velocity vs distance (sweeping d)

explorations.change: Set K = 500 and d = 2 Mpc, then change d to 4 Mpc.
explorations.observe: The predicted velocity doubles from 1000 km/s to 2000 km/s, and the ratio_check computation stays at 2.
explorations.why: At fixed K, v_corrected is proportional to d, so doubling distance doubles the predicted velocity. This is the linearity stated in the paper.

explorations.change: Keep d = 2 Mpc and raise K from 500 to 600 km/s/Mpc.
explorations.observe: The predicted velocity rises from 1000 km/s to 1200 km/s, and the line in the view becomes steeper.
explorations.why: Increasing K increases the slope of the line, so every distance maps to a larger predicted velocity. The paper's fitted values 465 and 513 bracket the rounded 500.

limitations: The displayed exact line is a simplified mean relation after solar-motion correction, not a fit to or reproduction of observed nebular velocities.
The plotted corrected velocities still include residuals; individual nebulae can deviate from the line because of peculiar motions.
The paper calls the linear relation a first approximation over a restricted distance range; do not extrapolate relativistically or infer universe age.
K = 500 is the paper's rounded historical teaching value, not a present-day measurement of the Hubble constant.
This source did not establish an exact modern cosmology; the lesson is about the 1929 linear correlation and its stated limitations.
